title: Calibration Laboratory CRM
subtitle: Lead-to-cash platform for a UAE medical-equipment calibration lab
description: A multi-branch platform covering the full lead-to-cash lifecycle for one of the few laboratories in the UAE with a dedicated lab for calibrating medical equipment. Sales, operations, procurement, finance and compliance in one system, with traceability across every approval and financial edit.
role: Lead developer. Sole author of 98% of both the backend and frontend repositories.
outcome: The largest system I have worked on, and the one that taught me the most. Delivered against a signed scope of work with contractual SLA and performance targets.
highlights: 18 business modules: sales CRM, clients, work orders, repairs, instruments, inventory, procurement, HRM, certificates, settings, IAM and audit logging. Every module feeds at least one other, so data entered once is referenced downstream instead of re-keyed.

Multi-branch tenancy where each branch operates with its own credentials, and every generated document carries the issuing branch's identity. A snapshot audit freezes counterparty details onto issued documents so a later edit to a vendor cannot rewrite history.
A maker-checker approval chain through Leads, Proposals and a single-transaction Accept and Convert that creates the client and raises the work order together, so the two can never diverge.
A shared PDF engine rendering nine document types across procurement and HRM, replacing the per-module one-offs that came before it.
Procurement end to end: vendors, purchase requisition, purchase order, goods received note, record purchase, purchase return, and a vendor payments ledger.

title: Hospital Management Systems
subtitle: Two live deployments on a shared modular core
description: Two hospital management platforms built and deployed for separate healthcare clients, sharing a common modular backend so improvements to auth, audit and permissions landed in both.
role: Joint lead with one colleague across backend and frontend. Primary author on both frontends.
outcome: Both are live. Building two products off one core showed me exactly which abstractions survive a second client and which were wishful thinking.
highlights: Shared modular monolith core: JWT auth with refresh tokens, role and permission based access control, and an append-only activity log recording actor, action, resource and a JSON detail payload.
A release notes system that surfaces what changed to users inside the product, rather than in an email nobody opens.
Frontend built on the internal Next.js template, which is where most of the template's rough edges were found and fixed.

title: Hospitality Service Marketplace
subtitle: Two-sided booking platform connecting providers, employers and job seekers
description: A marketplace where service providers, customers, employers and job seekers meet, with booking, referrals and provider management. This was the organisation's first real FastAPI project and the one where the house architecture was worked out.
role: Full-stack contributor across backend and frontend, alongside two colleagues. My first project at the company.
outcome: The project I learned the house patterns on, and the reason the conventions kit exists. Several rules in it were written because of bugs that shipped here first.
highlights: Booking and service-provider modules carrying the bulk of the domain logic, plus customer, employer, job seeker and referral flows.
Worked through the architectural iteration honestly: different modules landed on different patterns as the team learned, and the current best practice was written down rather than left implicit.
Live on its own domain with Celery workers and Flower monitoring in production.

title: Construction Project CRM
subtitle: Project management and operations for a construction firm
description: A CRM for running construction projects: clients, projects, operations tracking and the document trail around them, on the standard modular backend.
role: Full-stack contributor. Primary author on the frontend.
outcome: A straightforward brief delivered on the house stack, which is what the templates are for.
highlights: JWT auth with refresh tokens and RBAC, Celery background tasks with Flower monitoring, and S3-compatible object storage on DigitalOcean Spaces.
Prometheus metrics and rotating structured logs wired in from the start rather than added after the first incident.
Append-only activity log for the audit trail.

title: Sales CRM
subtitle: Pipeline and customer management
description: A sales CRM covering pipeline, customers and the reporting around them, scaffolded from the in-house CLI and finished on the standard stack.
role: Primary author on the frontend, contributor on the backend.
outcome: The first project generated from the internal CLI, which surfaced what the scaffolding was missing.
highlights: Frontend built and owned end to end.
Backend generated from the in-house FastAPI scaffolding and extended with the domain modules.

title: HRM Platform
subtitle: Employees, attendance, leave and payroll data
description: A human resource management platform covering employees, attendance, leave, salary, departments, designations, shifts, teams and holidays.
role: Sole developer. 29 of 29 backend commits and 51 of 53 frontend commits.
outcome: Built end to end on my own inside a tight window, which is the clearest test of whether the templates actually save time. They did.
highlights: Full HRM domain: employees, attendance, leave, salary, departments, designations, shifts, teams and holidays.
PDF generation with ReportLab, spreadsheet import and export via Pandas and openpyxl, and image processing with Pillow.
Rate limiting with slowapi, Prometheus instrumentation, and a pytest suite with pytest-asyncio and httpx.

title: Next.js Frontend Template
subtitle: The company standard for new frontends
description: An opinionated production template that new client frontends start from. I built and documented it on my own. It is not a starter kit, it is the argument for how we build frontends, written down so it survives me.
outcome: Now the default starting point for new projects. Writing the rules down forced me to justify each one, and several did not survive the writing.
highlights: 143 files across app routes, a data-view component layer, shared UI, permissions, forms and a typed API client.
Backend-for-frontend authentication: tokens live in httpOnly cookies and are never exposed to JavaScript. Route handlers proxy auth and inject the bearer token.
Built-in RBAC with four default roles and resource.action permission strings, gating both navigation and individual components.

17 numbered rule documents, each one topic, plus an architecture guide explaining how the pieces fit. A CLAUDE.md carries the guardrails and the anti-pattern list for AI assistants working in the repo.
Trimming support, so a project that does not need permissions, decimal money maths or dark mode can remove them cleanly instead of working around them.

title: Backend Conventions Kit
subtitle: Rules, traps and checklists for starting a backend
description: A portable folder you copy into a new backend on day one. Every rule in it was paid for once already, by a bug that shipped. The point of copying it is that you do not pay for them again.
outcome: The clearest thing I have written. It is what I would hand a new engineer before they open the code.
highlights: 17 concern guides, one per cross-cutting topic: permissions, migrations, caching, tenancy and scoping, dates and timezones, money and quantities, state machines, background jobs, audit logging, pagination, rate limiting, seeding, notifications, import and export, analytics, testing and the frontend contract.
A day-one checklist of roughly twenty decisions that are cheap now and very expensive in month six.
One owner per rule. A cross-cutting rule is written in full in exactly one place and appears everywhere else as a one-line summary with a link, so it cannot drift into eight disagreeing copies.
Every document carries a date stamp, and check_docs.py fails the commit when a link dies or a document goes stale. A document that lies is worse than no document.

title: Nadisa Solutions
subtitle: Career guidance platform for chemistry professionals
description: A live platform combining career guidance content, job discovery, contact workflows and a secure admin dashboard for a real business.
outcome: A real business runs on it, which is a different bar from a side project nobody depends on.
highlights: Next.js 16 and React 19 on the App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion and Radix UI.
Firebase Firestore, Authentication and Storage powering blogs, jobs, contact submissions and the admin dashboard.
Production concerns handled: SEO metadata, JSON-LD, sitemap generation, PWA readiness, mobile-first animation fallbacks and Core Web Vitals monitoring.

title: Visume
subtitle: AI video resume and hiring platform
description: A live hiring platform built during my internship at GRID R & D, where candidates record video answers and the system scores their technical responses to give employers a structured first screen.
role: Built the AI video-interview flow and worked across the MERN stack, MySQL, Prisma and AWS S3.
outcome: My first experience shipping something that strangers use without anyone explaining it to them first.
highlights: AI-scored video interview flow for technical screening.
Authentication, authorization and S3-backed file storage for candidate and employer data.

title: Code Eval AI
subtitle: AI-assisted code and interface review workspace
description: An evaluation workflow pairing AI-generated analysis with structured scoring and a reviewer-friendly interface for assessing code submissions.
outcome: An early attempt at making model output predictable enough to act on, rather than just interesting to read.
highlights: Gemini-backed analysis mapped to consistent scoring output.
PostgreSQL and Prisma managing submission state.

title: ClickTalk
subtitle: Realtime messaging
description: A realtime chat application with secure authentication, online presence and a lightweight interface.
outcome: Where I learned how much harder stateful realtime behaviour is than request and response.
highlights: Socket-based messaging with online presence tracking.
Authentication and authorization flows with Zustand-managed client state.

title: BookStore
subtitle: Catalogue and inventory interface
description: A Next.js application for browsing, managing and organising book inventory.
outcome: An early exercise in pairing a polished interface with real database-backed functionality.
highlights: PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM behind a typed Next.js frontend.
Authentication with NextAuth.

title: Secure OTP Authentication
subtitle: Passwordless access flow
description: A passwordless authentication flow built around OTP verification, session-aware access and usage analytics.
outcome: A focused look at the trade-off between security and how much friction a login can carry.
highlights: OTP verification with session handling.
Analytics interface for activity and usage patterns.
